91	Introduction
92	Training volume during resistance training (RT) is a key factor in determining
93	the strength, hypertrophy, neural and athletic performance adaptations that occur after a
94	training program (Kraemer and Ratamess 2004; Pareja-Blanco et al. 2017c).
95	Traditionally, it has been suggested that RT should be conducted to muscle failure in
96	order to maximize strength and muscle mass gains (Ahtiainen et al. 2003; Kraemer and
97	Ratamess 2004). However, an increasing number of investigations (Davies et al. 2016;
98	Gonzalez-Badillo et al. 2005; Izquierdo et al. 2006; Pareja-Blanco et al. 2017c;
99	For personal use only. This Just-IN manuscript is the accepted manuscript prior to copy editing and page composition. It may differ from the final official version of record.
100	Sampson and Groeller 2016) appear to indicate that completing the maximal number of
101	repetitions in each set may not be a necessary stimulus to produce greater increments in
102	muscle strength compared to lower training volumes. Indeed, training to muscle failure
103	induces a high level of mechanical, metabolic and hormonal stress (Gonzalez-Badillo et
104	al. 2016; Moran-Navarro et al. 2017; Pareja-Blanco et al. 2017b; Sanchez-Medina and
105	Gonzalez-Badillo 2011), and it appears that the continuous use of this type of RT results
106	in a significant decrement in the rate of force development (Andersen et al. 2010) and,
107	consequently, a reduction in the ability to perform high-speed actions such as jumps and
108	sprints (Pareja-Blanco et al. 2017c). However, although recent studies clearly suggest
109	discarding training to muscle failure, the optimal volume during RT for improving
110	performance in muscle strength and other motor skills is still unknown.
111	5
112	Page 6 of 47
113	Several authors have hypothesized that there may be a curvilinear relationship
114	Appl. Physiol. Nutr. Metab. Downloaded from www.nrcresearchpress.com by OHIO STATE UNIVERSITY on 05/07/20
115	(an inverted “U”-shaped curve) between training volume and gains in muscle strength
116	and physical performance (Busso 2003; Gonzalez-Badillo et al. 2005; Kuipers 1996).
117	This relationship indicates that there is a minimum volume (volume threshold) for each
118	load magnitude range to induce neuromuscular improvements. From that minimum
119	volume threshold, a progressive increase in training volume will be accompanied by an
120	increase in strength gains, up to a certain limit, beyond which an increase in training
121	volume will not produce additional benefits in terms of muscle strength. Even, if a
122	certain training volume value is exceeded, it is likely that gains in strength and physical
123	performance will decrease (Busso 2003; Gonzalez-Badillo et al. 2005; Kuipers 1996).
124	Thus, one of the main aims of coaches and sports scientists should be to look for the
125	minimum and maximum volume thresholds (numbers of repetitions per set) that
126	For personal use only. This Just-IN manuscript is the accepted manuscript prior to copy editing and page composition. It may differ from the final official version of record.
127	produce improvements in physical performance.
128	Studies analyzing acute mechanical, metabolic and hormonal responses to
129	different RT protocols (Gonzalez-Badillo et al. 2016; Moran-Navarro et al. 2017;
130	Pareja-Blanco et al. 2017b; Sanchez-Medina and Gonzalez-Badillo 2011) have shown
131	exponential increments in plasma ammonium, cortisol, prolactin (PRL), growth
132	hormone (GH) and creatine kinase (CK) concentrations, along with a decrease in heart
133	rate variability, when one half of the possible repetitions within a set is exceeded. These
134	changes are indicative of a high degree of fatigue, stress, muscle damage and muscle
135	catabolism, so it has been proposed that this volume limit (half of the possible
136	repetitions) should not be exceeded during RT when the aim is to improve
137	neuromuscular performance (Gonzalez-Badillo et al. 2016; Pareja-Blanco et al. 2017b;
138	Sanchez-Medina and Gonzalez-Badillo 2011). In accordance with this hypothesis, it has
139	6
140	Page 7 of 47
141	been found that performing half of the possible repetitions within each training set
142	Appl. Physiol. Nutr. Metab. Downloaded from www.nrcresearchpress.com by OHIO STATE UNIVERSITY on 05/07/20
143	produces similar or even higher increases in strength, power and physical performance
144	than those achieved after performing the maximum number of repetitions per set
145	(Izquierdo et al. 2006). Similarly, a recent study using a velocity-based RT approach
146	(Pareja-Blanco et al. 2017c) in full-squat exercise (SQ) showed that performing
147	repetitions until reaching a 20% velocity loss (VL) in the set [approximately half the
148	maximum possible number of repetitions per set (Rodriguez-Rosell et al. 2019)] was
149	more effective in inducing strength and vertical jump gains compared to perform
150	repetitions until reaching 40% VL in the set [repetitions to, or very close to, muscle
151	failure (Rodriguez-Rosell et al. 2019)], although the latter group resulted in greater
152	hypertrophic response. The results of these studies (Izquierdo et al. 2006; Pareja-Blanco
153	et al. 2017c) seem to confirm the hypothesis that performing more than half of the
154	For personal use only. This Just-IN manuscript is the accepted manuscript prior to copy editing and page composition. It may differ from the final official version of record.
155	possible repetitions during RT does not produce greater benefits for neuromuscular
156	performance. However, these previous studies (Izquierdo et al. 2006; Pareja-Blanco et
157	al. 2017c) only analyzed two repetition ranges: ~20% VL (half of the repetitions
158	possible) vs. ~40% VL (muscle failure), leaving a wide spectrum of percentage VL in
159	the set unanalyzed. Therefore, whether velocity losses lower or slightly higher than 20%
160	induce better beneficial effects on physical performance still remains unknown.
161	It has been suggested that changes in hormonal homeostasis during RT play a
162	relevant role in the synthesis of proteins and the development of muscle strength
163	(Hoppeler 2016; Kraemer and Ratamess 2005; Marx et al. 2001). Acute hormonal
164	responses after different RT protocols have been widely analyzed (Gonzalez-Badillo et
165	al. 2016; Pareja-Blanco et al. 2017b; Rubin et al. 2005), whereas the chronic effects
166	have received less scientific attention (Kraemer and Ratamess 2005). This may be
167	7
168	Page 8 of 47
169	because most hormones show a strong acute response that is reversed several hours after
170	Appl. Physiol. Nutr. Metab. Downloaded from www.nrcresearchpress.com by OHIO STATE UNIVERSITY on 05/07/20
171	exercise (Gonzalez-Badillo et al. 2016; Pareja-Blanco et al. 2017b). However, it also
172	seems that RT maintained for long periods could produce alterations in resting
173	hormonal concentrations, indicating that these hormones could also be used as
174	biomarkers of chronic muscle stress induced by RT (Kraemer and Ratamess 2005).
175	Most studies analyzing chronic changes in baseline hormonal concentrations have used
176	training protocols conducted to muscle failure in each set (Ahtiainen et al. 2003;
177	Kraemer and Ratamess 2005; Kraemer et al. 1999), showing different results depending
178	on the hormone analyzed and the load magnitude used. To the authors' knowledge, there
179	has been only one study (Izquierdo et al. 2006) comparing the effect of two RT
180	programs differing in the number of repetitions completed in each training set on resting
181	hormonal concentration. This study showed increments in insulin-like growth-factor 1
182	For personal use only. This Just-IN manuscript is the accepted manuscript prior to copy editing and page composition. It may differ from the final official version of record.
183	(IGF-1) and no changes in testosterone and cortisol concentrations for the muscle failure
184	training group, whereas the group who trained performing half of the maximal possible
185	repetitions showed increments in testosterone and decrements in cortisol concentration,
186	which is associated with a positive anabolic-catabolic balance (Izquierdo et al. 2006).
187	Thus, it seems that changes in serum hormonal concentrations in resting conditions are
188	related to the volume or level of effort induced during RT. However, considering that
189	we only know of one study with these characteristics, it appears that further
190	investigations are needed to clarify the chronic effect of RT with different degrees of
191	fatigue (i.e., magnitudes of VL) on resting hormonal concentrations.
192	On the other hand, increments in muscle strength are also associated with
193	changes in neural factors, mainly in the first weeks of training, where the increase in
194	strength is not related to the morphological changes in the muscle (Moritani and deVries
195	8
196	Page 9 of 47
197	1979). Evidence of adaptive changes in neural function with RT have been analyzed
198	Appl. Physiol. Nutr. Metab. Downloaded from www.nrcresearchpress.com by OHIO STATE UNIVERSITY on 05/07/20
199	using surface electromyogram (EMG). Several studies have showed changes in EMG
200	variables after an RT program, even in athletes highly trained in RT, which indicates the
201	high level of plasticity of the neural system (Hoppeler 2016). Most studies have
202	analyzed the changes in muscle EMG during isometric contractions or against a 1RM
203	load, showing significant changes in EMG amplitude (RMS, integrated EMG, mean
204	average voltage) or mean and median power frequency after different RT programs
205	(Aagaard et al. 2002; Buckthorpe et al. 2015; Sampson and Groeller 2016; Ullrich et al.
206	2015). However, to the best of our knowledge, no studies have yet analyzed the changes
207	in EMG variables against different absolute loads following RT with different degrees
208	of fatigue, quantified using the VL achieved in the set.
209	For personal use only. This Just-IN manuscript is the accepted manuscript prior to copy editing and page composition. It may differ from the final official version of record.
210	Therefore, in an attempt to obtain further knowledge about the minimum
211	stimulus required to induce strength improvements and the physiological factors that
212	determine changes in physical performance, the aim of the present study was to
213	compare the effects of two RT programs with different degrees of fatigue or levels of
214	effort in each set (10% vs. 30% velocity loss) on neuromuscular performance and
215	hormonal responses. Based on previous studies, we hypothesized that improvements in
216	strength and motor skill performance will be similar or even greater for the RT program
217	allowing only a 10% VL compared to 30% VL, which will also be accompanied by an
218	increase in muscular electrical activity. In contrast, it is expected that RT with 30% VL
219	will induce greater muscle damage and worse anabolic-catabolic balance than RT with
220	10% VL.

230	to their estimated one-repetition maximum (1RM) in the SQ exercise and then randomly
231	assigned into two groups depending on the magnitude of VL allowed during the set:

233	intervention, one participant from the VL10% was excluded from the study. Thus, 12
234	participants in the VL10% group (age: 22.8±3.1 years, body mass: 75.1±10.3 kg, height:

Abstract
This study aimed to compare the effects of two resistance training (RT) programs with
different velocity losses allowed in each set: 10% (VL10%) vs. 30% (VL30%) on
neuromuscular performance and hormonal response. Twenty-five young healthy males
were randomly assigned into two groups: VL10% (n=12) or VL30% (n=13). Subjects
followed a velocity-based RT program for 8 weeks (2 sessions per week) using only the
full-squat (SQ) exercise at 70-85% 1RM. Repetition velocity was recorded in all
training sessions. A 20-m running sprint, countermovement jump (CMJ), 1RM, muscle
endurance and EMG during SQ exercise, and resting hormonal concentrations were
assessed before and after RT program. Both groups showed similar improvements in

set as low as 10% are enough to achieve significant improvements in neuromuscular

Introduction
Training volume during resistance training (RT) is a key factor in determining
the strength, hypertrophy, neural and athletic performance adaptations that occur after a
training program (Kraemer and Ratamess 2004; Pareja-Blanco et al. 2017c).
Traditionally, it has been suggested that RT should be conducted to muscle failure in
order to maximize strength and muscle mass gains (Ahtiainen et al. 2003; Kraemer and
Ratamess 2004). However, an increasing number of investigations (Davies et al. 2016;
Gonzalez-Badillo et al. 2005; Izquierdo et al. 2006; Pareja-Blanco et al. 2017c;

Sampson and Groeller 2016) appear to indicate that completing the maximal number of
repetitions in each set may not be a necessary stimulus to produce greater increments in
muscle strength compared to lower training volumes. Indeed, training to muscle failure
induces a high level of mechanical, metabolic and hormonal stress (Gonzalez-Badillo et
al. 2016; Moran-Navarro et al. 2017; Pareja-Blanco et al. 2017b; Sanchez-Medina and
Gonzalez-Badillo 2011), and it appears that the continuous use of this type of RT results
in a significant decrement in the rate of force development (Andersen et al. 2010) and,
consequently, a reduction in the ability to perform high-speed actions such as jumps and
sprints (Pareja-Blanco et al. 2017c). However, although recent studies clearly suggest
discarding training to muscle failure, the optimal volume during RT for improving
performance in muscle strength and other motor skills is still unknown.

and physical performance (Busso 2003; Gonzalez-Badillo et al. 2005; Kuipers 1996).
This relationship indicates that there is a minimum volume (volume threshold) for each
load magnitude range to induce neuromuscular improvements. From that minimum
volume threshold, a progressive increase in training volume will be accompanied by an
increase in strength gains, up to a certain limit, beyond which an increase in training
volume will not produce additional benefits in terms of muscle strength. Even, if a
certain training volume value is exceeded, it is likely that gains in strength and physical
performance will decrease (Busso 2003; Gonzalez-Badillo et al. 2005; Kuipers 1996).
Thus, one of the main aims of coaches and sports scientists should be to look for the
minimum and maximum volume thresholds (numbers of repetitions per set) that

Materials and methods
Participants
Twenty-six healthy men volunteered to take part in this study. Participants were
physically active sport science students with RT experience ranging from 1 to 3 years
(1-3 sessions per week) and they had been injury-free for at least 6 months before
participating in this study. After initial evaluation, participants were matched according
to their estimated one-repetition maximum (1RM) in the SQ exercise and then randomly
assigned into two groups depending on the magnitude of VL allowed during the set:
10% (VL10%) or 30% (VL30%). As a result of illness not related to the training
intervention, one participant from the VL10% was excluded from the study. Thus, 12
participants in the VL10% group (age: 22.8±3.1 years, body mass: 75.1±10.3 kg, height:

74.0±9.1 kg, height: 1.76±0.07 m) remained for statistical analyses. No physical
limitations, health problems, or musculoskeletal injuries that could affect the testing
were reported. The study was conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki and
was approved by the Local Ethics Committee. After being informed of the purpose and
experimental procedures, the participants signed a written informed consent form prior
to participation.

effects of two RT programs, differing only in the VL allowed in each training set (10%
vs. 30%), on physical performance, hormonal responses and changes in muscle EMG.

All participants carried out an 8-week velocity-based RT program involving 2
sessions per week (16 total sessions), using only the SQ exercise. The full-squat
exercise was chosen as training exercise because this type of exercise induce greater
neuromuscular and functional adaptations and lower pain than half- or quarter-squat
after prolonged RT period (Hartmann et al. 2013; Pallares et al. 2019). Training
variables such as relative intensity (70%-85% 1RM), number of sets (three), recovery
time between sets (4 min) and recovery time between sessions (72 hours) were the same

velocity relationship for the SQ exercise (Sánchez-Medina et al. 2017). Thus, a target
MPV to be attained in the first (usually the fastest) repetition of the first exercise set in
each training session was used as an estimation of percentage of 1RM, as follows: ~0.84

m·s-1 (~85% 1RM). Consequently, before starting the first set in each training session,
adjustments in the proposed load (kg) were made when needed so that the velocity of
the first repetition matched the programmed velocity (± 0.03 m·s-1). Once the load (kg)
was adjusted, it was maintained for the 3 training sets. Volume in each training set was
objectively determined through the magnitude of VL attained over the set (calculated as
the percent loss in MPV from the fastest to the slowest repetition) (Rodriguez-Rosell et

According to this method, depending on the training group, participants performed

Standard statistical methods were used for the calculation of means, standard

Pre)/Pooled SD. The ES for changes between the VL10% and VL30% groups for each

Data for all variables analyzed were homogeneous and normally distributed (p>0.05).
Compliance with the training program was 100% for both experimental groups. No

Discussion
The main finding of the present study was that a RT program performing
repetitions at maximal intended velocity until reaching a 10% VL in the set compared to
For personal use only. This Just-IN manuscript is the accepted manuscript prior to copy editing and page composition. It may differ from the final official version of record.
30% in the SQ exercise produced similar, or even greater (depending on the variable
assessed), increments in muscle strength, muscle endurance, jump and sprint
performance, as well as EMG activity. In addition, the VL30% resulted in greater
chronic muscle damage determined by the percentage of increments in TnT plasma
concentration. Therefore, in accordance with previous investigations (Pareja-Blanco et
al. 2017a; Pareja-Blanco et al. 2017c), the results of the present study suggest that the
degree of fatigue induced during each training set (quantified by the VL) is a
determining factor in modulating the neuromuscular adaptations that occur during RT.
Specifically, the present study appears to indicate RT allowing a 10% VL in the set is a
more efficient than RT with 30% VL for improving physical performance
(Supplementary Material S3).

no significant differences between groups were found, the VL10% resulted in greater
percentage changes and intra-group ESs than VL30% for most variables, particularly in
MPV attained with light loads (AV>1 and MPV30-50). It is important to note that these
changes occurred despite the fact that the VL10% group performed, on average, less

training program (109.6±12.0 vs. 228.0±76.6 repetitions for VL10% and VL30%,
respectively). These results were especially relevant in the fatigue test, as it has been
postulated that performing a greater number of repetitions per set during RT should

with different numbers of repetitions per set also showed no significant differences

should be to find more efficient RT methods; that is, obtaining the highest possible
gains with the lowest degree of fatigue. Coinciding with our results, several studies have

VL experienced during each training set directly influences functional, neural and

neuromuscular performance. However, the present study also suggests that VL in the set
as low as 10% (2-4 repetitions) may be similar to or even more beneficial than higher
levels of VL for obtaining increments in physical performance. These findings are of
great practical relevance for those athletes aiming to improve their ability to apply force
over short time periods without an excessive degree of fatigue that could interfere with
other specific technical-tactical skills, and avoiding excessive muscle hypertrophy that
could produce an increase in body weight that would negatively affect performance.

  "id": "Q68",
  "sourceFile": "Velocity-Based Training With Weightlifting Derivatives - Barbell and System Velocity Comparisons.pdf",
  "decision": "INCLUDE",
  "exclusionReason": "",
  "degradedReason": "",
  "doiMissing": false,
  "identityCheck": "PDF title 'Velocity-Based Training With Weightlifting Derivatives: Barbell and System Velocity Comparisons' (Suchomel et al., J Strength Cond Res) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
  "confidence": "high",
  "studyDesign": "Methodological / Validation Study",
  "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
  "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Training & Performance"],
  "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
  "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
  "populations": ["Adult / Recreational"],
  "evidenceSummary": "Repeated-measures study in 14 resistance-trained men who were not competitive weightlifters. Each performed single repetitions of the jump shrug, hang high pull, hang power clean, hang clean pull and countermovement shrug across 4 to 7 loads (20% to 140% of hang power clean 1RM), measured with a barbell linear position transducer and a force platform. The authors report that mean and peak barbell velocities were significantly greater than system velocities at every exercise and load (p < 0.001, Hedges g at least 1.49), and conclude the two measures should not be substituted for one another.",
  "screeningLimitations": "Only single repetitions were tested, not sets, and several loads (20% to 40% of hang power clean 1RM) are lighter than these lifts are usually prescribed. The sample was 14 men who were not competitive weightlifters, so generalization to women, weightlifters or other groups is limited. System velocity CVs exceeded 10% at some light loads (for example, 11.7% for the jump shrug at 20%).",
  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the barbell-system gap as a reason to treat the two velocity measures as interchangeable, or to set loads for these pulls from mean barbell velocity zones built for other lifts. The authors say the measures are distinct and that mean velocity may not guide load prescription for these pulls.",
  "paper": {
    "year": 2025,
    "citation": "Suchomel TJ, Kissick CR, Techmanski BS, Mann JB, Comfort P. Velocity-Based Training With Weightlifting Derivatives: Barbell and System Velocity Comparisons. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2025;39(2):135-146.",
    "doi": "10.1519/jsc.0000000000004962",
    "abstract": "Compared mean and peak barbell velocity with system velocity (athlete plus load) during five weightlifting derivatives across a range of relative loads in 14 resistance-trained men, using force platforms and linear position transducers.",
    "tldr": "In resistance-trained men, barbell velocity was consistently and substantially higher than system velocity across five weightlifting pulls and every load tested. Treat the two as different measures, and do not swap one for the other when setting loads.",
    "methods": "Repeated-measures design. Participants completed six sessions over about two weeks, starting with a 1RM hang power clean test, then exercise sessions in randomized order. Single repetitions were performed at 20% to 100% (jump shrug and hang high pull), 20% to 80% (hang power clean), and 20% to 140% (hang clean pull and countermovement shrug) of hang power clean 1RM. Barbell velocity came from a linear position transducer and system velocity from force-platform integration. Reliability was assessed with ICC and CV, and differences with repeated-measures ANOVA and Hedges g.",
    "findings": "Mean and peak barbell velocity exceeded system velocity at every exercise and load (p < 0.001, Hedges g at least 1.49). For example, the hang power clean at 20% gave mean barbell velocity 1.46 m/s against system velocity 0.62 m/s. Most system velocities were below 1.00 m/s, except the jump shrug at 20% to 60%. Reliability was mostly good to excellent for both measures (ICCs mostly 0.84 to 0.99), with system velocity CVs above 10% at some light loads.",
    "limitations": "Single repetitions rather than sets, some loads lighter than typical prescription, and a small sample of resistance-trained men who were not competitive weightlifters. System velocity was less reliable at light loads. The authors note that subject height and limb length may affect barbell velocity, and call for research across sets and populations.",
    "practicalImplications": "Use peak velocity to characterize these weightlifting derivatives. Barbell velocity may matter most for weightlifters, while system velocity may be more relevant for non-weightlifters who use derivatives in training. Because the transition phase limits how well mean velocity reflects load, it should not be the main basis for load prescription in these pulls.",
    "athleteDev": "For exercise and load selection, use peak velocity to characterize the pulling derivatives. Barbell velocity may guide weightlifters, and system velocity may be more relevant for non-weightlifters. Mean velocity may be a poor basis for load prescription in these lifts.",
    "rtp": "The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested single repetitions of pulling lifts in a lab with resistance-trained men and did not include injured athletes or return-to-play testing."
  }
}

Abstract
Suchomel, TJ, Kissick, CR, Techmanski, BS, Mann, JB, and Comfort, P. Velocity-based training with weightlifting derivatives:
Barbell and system velocity comparisons. J Strength Cond Res 39(2): 135–146, 2025—The aim of this study was to examine the
differences in barbell and system (i.e., subject + load) velocity during weightlifting derivatives performed across a spectrum of
relative loads. 14 resistance-trained men participated in 6 testing sessions, which included 1 repetition maximum hang power clean
(HPC) testing and individual jump shrug (JS), hang high pull (HHP), HPC, hang clean pull (HCP), and countermovement shrug (CMS)
sessions. The order of the exercise testing sessions was randomized and required the subjects to perform either JS, HHP, HPC,
HCP, or CMS repetitions while standing on a force platform with a linear position transducer attached to the barbell. The JS and
HHP were performed with 20, 40, 60, 80, and 100% of their 1 repetition maximum HPC, HPC with 20, 40, 60, and 80% 1RM, and
the HCP and CMS performed with 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, and 140% 1RM. Mean and peak barbell and system velocities were
determined across all exercises and loads using either 2 3 5, 2 3 4, or 2 3 7 repeated measures ANOVA depending on the number
of loads performed. Significantly (p , 0.001) and meaningfully (g $ 1.49) greater mean and peak barbell velocities existed at every
exercise and load combination compared with the mean and peak system velocities produced. Barbell and system velocity are
distinct characteristics that should not be substituted for one another. Owing to the characteristics of the transition phase, mean
barbell and system velocity may not provide strength and conditioning practitioners with meaningful information related to load
prescription.
Key Words: jump shrug, hang high pull, hang power clean, hang pull, countermovement shrug, Olympic weightlifting

  "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
  "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
  "evidenceSummary": "Review of 14 double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trials of supraphysiologic vitamin C in athletes and active adults, identified by a PubMed search of 2012 to 2022 (97 articles screened). Most trials combined vitamin C with vitamin E or another antioxidant. The authors report that three trials found lower muscle damage markers with vitamin C-containing supplements, while the other 11 found neutral or negative effects on muscle damage, performance, soreness or training adaptation.",
  "screeningLimitations": "The review is a single PubMed search with a narrow keyword set and no meta-analysis or formal quality grading. Most of the 14 trials had fewer than 60 participants, and most combined vitamin C with other antioxidants, so vitamin C effects cannot be separated. Populations are mixed, from elderly men and students to elite taekwondo athletes.",
  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this as a blanket ban on vitamin C for all athletes, when most trials used vitamin C with vitamin E, the sample sizes were small, and the recommendation rests on a mixed set of studies.",
  "paper": {
    "year": 2023,
    "citation": "Rogers DR, Lawlor DJ, Moeller JL. Vitamin C Supplementation and Athletic Performance: A Review. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2023;22(7):255-259.",
    "doi": "10.1249/jsr.0000000000001083",
    "abstract": "Reviews 14 randomized placebo-controlled trials of high-dose vitamin C in athletes and active people, most combined with other antioxidants, on muscle damage, performance and training adaptation.",
    "tldr": "Across 14 placebo-controlled trials, high-dose vitamin C showed no consistent benefit for performance or soreness, and some trials reported blunted training adaptations when taken with vitamin E. The authors advise against long-term high-dose vitamin C and recommend antioxidants from a nutrient-rich diet.",
    "methods": "PubMed search for 2012 to 2022 using the terms vitamin C, ascorbic acid, athlete and performance, yielding 97 articles. Inclusion required a double-blind placebo-controlled randomized trial of supraphysiologic vitamin C (alone or mixed) and an exercise performance or muscle damage outcome. Fourteen trials were included. No pooled analysis was done.",
    "findings": "Three trials (Askari 2012; Chou 2018; Gillam 2022) reported lower muscle damage markers, such as creatine kinase or myoglobin, with vitamin C plus quercetin or vitamin E. The other trials found no benefit for performance, soreness or perceived exertion. Long-term trials of vitamin C plus vitamin E found that placebo groups had larger gains in lean mass and muscle thickness in older men and in strength and hypertrophy in recreational weightlifters, and greater mitochondrial biogenesis markers in placebo groups in two endurance-exercise studies (Paulsen 2014; Morrison 2015). A combined antioxidant taken before exercise reduced cycling power output in hyperoxia.",
    "limitations": "Single search and no formal quality appraisal. Most trials co-supplemented vitamin C with vitamin E or other antioxidants, so vitamin C effects cannot be isolated. Sample sizes are small. The table and text disagree on the sample for the 10-week Martinez-Ferran trial (32 vs 12) and on the vitamin E dose in the Paulsen trial (235 vs 325 mg). Populations and doses vary widely.",
    "practicalImplications": "Athletes asking about high-dose vitamin C for performance or recovery should be told the trial evidence is inconsistent, and that the authors advise against long-term high-dose supplementation because it may blunt training adaptations. Diet is the recommended source of antioxidants. Short-term use around competition is less well studied and needs its own assessment.",
    "athleteDev": "For training adaptation, the review points to possible blunting of strength and endurance gains with long-term high-dose vitamin C plus vitamin E, so staff should not recommend it during training blocks. Acute high-dose use has not shown a consistent performance benefit.",
    "rtp": "The review contains no return-to-sport or injury-recovery trials. Three small trials reported lower muscle damage markers after exercise, but they were not injury studies, and the authors do not recommend long-term high-dose use. These findings cannot support rehabilitation or return-to-sport use."
  }
}

{
  "id": "Q70",
  "sourceFile": "Vitamin D for improved bone health and prevention of stress fractures - A review of the literature.pdf",
  "decision": "INCLUDE",
  "exclusionReason": "",
  "degradedReason": "",
  "doiMissing": false,
  "identityCheck": "PDF title 'Vitamin D for Improved Bone Health and Prevention of Stress Fractures: A Review of the Literature' (Lawley, Syrop and Fredericson, Current Sports Medicine Reports) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
  "confidence": "high",
  "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
  "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
  "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Nutrition & Hydration"],
  "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Nutrition"],
  "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
  "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
  "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of vitamin D status, bone health and stress fractures, drawing on trials, cohort and case-control studies in children, adults, military recruits and some athletes. The authors report a consistent but heterogeneous association between vitamin D status and stress fracture, with a meta-analysis of eight military studies finding lower 25(OH)D in stress fracture cases (mean difference -2.44 ng/mL, 95% CI -4.05 to -0.84). They recommend vitamin D3 to maintain status in athletes at high stress-fracture risk, but say the data do not support a specific dose or target level for athletes.",
  "screeningLimitations": "No search method is described, so the selection of studies cannot be checked. The authors note that placebo-controlled RCTs in athletes are scarce, and most athlete evidence is observational. Many bone-outcome trials were in children, postmenopausal women or older adults, and the stress-fracture meta-analysis used military personnel rather than sport athletes. Vitamin D thresholds differ across organizations and no validated assay is available.",
  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this as proof that vitamin D supplementation prevents stress fractures in athletes. The athlete evidence is mainly observational, the authors say no dose or target level is supported for athletes, and the large meta-analysis they cite found no fracture prevention with supplementation in older adults.",
  "paper": {
    "year": 2020,
    "citation": "Lawley R, Syrop IP, Fredericson M. Vitamin D for Improved Bone Health and Prevention of Stress Fractures: A Review of the Literature. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2020;19(6):202-208.",
    "doi": "10.1249/jsr.0000000000000718",
    "abstract": "Reviews vitamin D physiology, status measurement and bone health, then the evidence linking vitamin D status and supplementation with stress fractures in adolescents, military recruits and athletes.",
    "tldr": "Vitamin D status and stress fracture risk appear linked in athletes and recruits, but the studies are heterogeneous and mostly observational. Vitamin D3 is reasonable to maintain status in high-risk athletes, but the review does not set a dose or target level for them.",
    "methods": "Narrative literature review. The article does not describe a search strategy, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal.",
    "findings": "Athletes, especially indoor and endurance athletes, often have low 25(OH)D. A meta-analysis of eight military studies (2,634 personnel) found lower 25(OH)D in stress fracture cases. In a Royal Marine cohort, low baseline 25(OH)D was linked to stress fracture risk. In a British Army study, recovery from lower-limb stress fracture took about 10 weeks with sufficient 25(OH)D, 12 with insufficient and 13 with deficient levels. In a Navy trial, calcium plus vitamin D reduced stress fracture incidence by about 20% (no statistics given in the text). Supplementation trials of bone density in children and adults are mixed, and a meta-analysis of 81 RCTs found no clear fracture or BMD benefit in older adults.",
    "limitations": "No search method or quality appraisal is described. Athlete evidence is mostly observational and small. Vitamin D thresholds differ by organization, and the authors note that 25(OH)D may not be the best marker. The review states that the athlete data are not strong enough to set a dose or target.",
    "practicalImplications": "Consider checking vitamin D status in athletes at high stress-fracture risk, such as indoor or endurance athletes, military-type trainees, and those with prior fracture. The authors suggest vitamin D3 supplementation to maintain status in such athletes, with doses of 800 to 2000 IU daily cited from the general literature rather than athlete trials.",
    "athleteDev": "The review does not support a dose or target serum level for athletic performance. It cites Cannell's suggestion that 50 ng/mL may be ideal for performance, but the authors say the athlete data are not strong enough to set a dose or target for bone health.",
    "rtp": "The only recovery data are military: recruits with sufficient 25(OH)D recovered from lower-limb stress fractures faster than those insufficient or deficient. This does not give a return-to-sport protocol, and the review cannot set return-to-play criteria or a dosing plan for an injured athlete."
  }
}

  "decision": "INCLUDE",
  "exclusionReason": "",
  "degradedReason": "",
  "doiMissing": false,
  "identityCheck": "PDF title 'Whole-Body Cryotherapy in Sports Medicine' (Patel, Bakshi, Freehill and Awan, Current Sports Medicine Reports) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
  "confidence": "high",
  "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
  "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",
  "domains": ["Recovery & Readiness", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
  "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Performance"],
  "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
  "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
  "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of whole-body cryotherapy (WBC) in sports medicine, covering inflammation, muscle damage, bone, blood, hormone and lipid markers, functional recovery, and clinical use in arthritis and adhesive capsulitis. The authors report mixed results for creatine kinase and blood markers, some anti-inflammatory and lipid changes, and no clear performance or recovery benefit in most controlled trials, with recovery evidence described as weak but supportive.",
  "screeningLimitations": "No search method or quality appraisal is described, so the selection of studies cannot be checked. Many cited trials are small, uncontrolled or laboratory-based, and they use different temperatures and durations. The samples mix athletes with patients, military students and overweight men. The clinical data are mostly in arthritis and shoulder conditions, not injured athletes.",
  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the anti-inflammatory and lipid findings as evidence that WBC speeds recovery or improves performance. The authors say most controlled trials found no functional or performance benefit and that the recovery evidence is weak.",
  "paper": {
    "year": 2019,
    "citation": "Patel K, Bakshi N, Freehill MT, Awan TM. Whole-Body Cryotherapy in Sports Medicine. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2019;18(4):136-140.",
    "doi": "10.1249/jsr.0000000000000584",
    "abstract": "Reviews whole-body cryotherapy in sports medicine, covering its proposed use for injury prevention and for reducing inflammation after exercise, its physiological effects, safety and contraindications, and clinical use.",
    "tldr": "Whole-body cryotherapy shows some anti-inflammatory and lipid effects, but most controlled trials find no benefit for performance or functional recovery. The authors suggest using it only as a supplement to recovery in people without contraindications, under skilled supervision.",
    "methods": "Narrative literature review. The article does not describe a search strategy, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal.",
    "findings": "Inflammation: one study reported that cryotherapy before exercise prevented IL-6 spikes in volleyball players, and another reported a larger TNF decrease than passive recovery after repeated daily sessions. Muscle damage: creatine kinase results are mixed, with a 34% decrease in kayakers in one study and no difference in trained runners in another. Blood and hormones: hemoglobin fell in some groups (for example, 15.06 to 14.70 g/dL after seven days in 27 rugby players), though other studies found no change, and norepinephrine rose after single sessions. Lipids: triglycerides and LDL fell and HDL rose in some trials of active men. Functional recovery: most controlled trials found no benefit, though a few reported better shot accuracy in tennis players and better acute recovery in endurance athletes.",
    "limitations": "No search method or quality appraisal is described. Most studies are small, and many are uncontrolled or laboratory-based. Exposure protocols vary in temperature and duration. The authors note the evidence for functional recovery and performance is limited and mixed, and that high-quality clinical research is needed.",
    "practicalImplications": "Whole-body cryotherapy should be given only with skilled supervision and after screening for contraindications, such as Raynaud disease, uncontrolled hypertension, cardiovascular disease and claustrophobia. Use it as an adjunct to recovery, not as a performance aid, since the authors judge the recovery evidence weak. Expect inconsistent effects on creatine kinase and hemoglobin.",
    "athleteDev": "The review does not support a performance benefit from whole-body cryotherapy. A few trials report better shot accuracy in tennis players or better acute recovery in endurance athletes, but most controlled trials show no effect on performance or functional recovery.",
    "rtp": "No return-to-sport trials are reported. Clinical data cover shoulder adhesive capsulitis (WBC plus physical therapy improved pain and range of motion more than physical therapy alone after four weeks) and arthritis, mostly in uncontrolled or review-level studies. The authors list cardiovascular disease, cold intolerance and other conditions as contraindications, so these data cannot set return-to-play criteria."
  }
}

  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this as evidence that CBD treats osteoarthritis, concussion or pain in athletes, when the cited support is mostly preclinical or non-athlete and the authors do not recommend CBD for concussion.",

    "year": 2021,
    "citation": "Naik H, Trojian TH. Therapeutic Potential for Cannabinoids in Sports Medicine: Current Literature Review. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2021;20(7):345-350.",
    "doi": "10.1249/jsr.0000000000000858",
    "abstract": "The review compares cannabidiol and delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol through the endocannabinoid system and summarizes their theoretical benefits and current U.S. legal status for common sports medicine conditions, to help clinicians answer questions from athletes and active patients.",
    "tldr": "This is a clinician guide rather than trial evidence. Cannabidiol shows anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects mainly in animal and in vitro work, and human sports medicine trials are lacking. The authors do not recommend CBD for concussion and do not recommend medical marijuana containing THC.",
    "methods": "Narrative literature review. The article does not describe a search strategy, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal.",
    "findings": "Covers CB1, CB2, TRPV1, serotonin and GPR55 pharmacology. For osteoarthritis, cannabinoid receptors are found in cartilage and synovium, and the authors cite mostly preclinical work suggesting pain relief and possible disease modification, while noting CBD is not an FDA-approved treatment. For concussion, the authors state that trials do not exist and they do not recommend use. CBD had little effect on anxiety under low stress and mixed effects under stress; one study found 300 mg more anxiolytic than 150 or 600 mg, and another found 600 mg increased anxiety in a high-paranoia group. Cardiovascular findings are inconsistent, and the cited studies were done at rest rather than during exercise.",
    "limitations": "The review is narrative and unsystematic, so the choice of evidence is not transparent. Most mechanistic and chronic pain support is preclinical, and human trials, dosing, safety and long-term effects remain unresolved in sports medicine. Adverse effects listed (drug interactions, liver enzyme elevation, diarrhea, fatigue, somnolence) come from epilepsy and psychiatric populations. Legal and market content is U.S.-specific and reflects 2020-2021 sources.",
    "practicalImplications": "Expect athletes and active patients to ask about CBD for osteoarthritis, pain, concussion and pre-competition anxiety. Explain that the evidence is mostly animal or in vitro, that CBD is not recommended for concussion, and that the authors advise against medical marijuana containing THC because nonprescription THC products are not federally legal. The authors' only dosing comment is that 600 mg appears a poor choice for performance anxiety, which comes from non-athlete studies.",
    "athleteDev": "The review contains no performance outcome data in athletes. Its cardiovascular and anxiety evidence is resting or non-sport based, and the authors state that CBD has not been studied for sports performance anxiety. It cannot support a performance or pre-competition dosing recommendation.",
    "rtp": "This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It contains no trials of cannabinoids for concussion or injury recovery, and the authors do not recommend CBD for concussion at this time."

    "status": "CORRECTED",
    "changes": [
      "paper.findings: anxiety evidence described as 'inconsistent results at low stress' -> little effect under low stress and mixed effects under stress, with the 300 mg vs 150/600 mg U-shaped result ('Under low-stress conditions, the effect of CBD has had little influence on anxiety'; 'several studies have shown no CBD effect on anxiety in this similar situation')",

      "paper.limitations: added that adverse-effect data come from epilepsy and psychiatric studies ('In vivo review in studies done for epilepsy and psychiatric disorders')",
      "paper.practicalImplications: replaced 'pre-competition dosing should not be based on this review' with the authors' actual dosing statement ('it would appear that 600 mg of CBD is not a good choice')"
    ],
    "residualConcerns": "Identity, DOI (Crossref match) and year 2021 all agree. Clinically sensitive topic (concussion, cannabinoid medication and anti-doping-adjacent questions); the review predates later CBD guidance, so staff should check current regulations.",
    "spotCheckPriority": "high"
  }
}

{
  "id": "Q66",
  "sourceFile": "Training Impulse and Session Ratings of Perceived Exertion as Perceived by Athletes and Observed by Coaches During Preseason Football Camp.pdf",
  "decision": "INCLUDE",
  "exclusionReason": "",
  "degradedReason": "",
  "doiMissing": false,
  "identityCheck": "PDF title 'Training Impulse and Session Ratings of Perceived Exertion as Perceived by Athletes and Observed by Coaches During Preseason Football Camp' (Smith-Hale et al., J Strength Cond Res) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
  "confidence": "high",
  "studyDesign": "Methodological / Validation Study",
  "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
  "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Training & Performance", "Recovery & Readiness"],
  "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
  "sports": ["American Football"],
  "populations": ["Collegiate"],
  "evidenceSummary": "Prospective study of 24 NCAA Division II football athletes (6 first-year, 18 returning) and 2 coaches over the first 6 days of preseason camp. It compares heart-rate training impulse (Edwards TRIMP, from chest-strap monitors) with session RPE load rated by athletes and by one football coach and one strength and conditioning coach. The authors report significant but low-to-moderate correlations (athletes r = 0.62, football coach r = 0.68, strength and conditioning coach r = 0.49), stronger in first-year athletes, and conclude the measures are not interchangeable.",
  "screeningLimitations": "Agreement was assessed with correlations only, not bias or limits of agreement, and the 139 observations are repeated measures on 24 athletes from one team. Each coach role is a single person, so coach findings describe two individuals, not coach types. Maximal heart rate was mostly estimated (220 minus age), and the paper has several internal numerical inconsistencies.",
  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read these correlations as showing that coach observation or athlete ratings can replace heart-rate monitoring, or that football coaches judge load better than strength coaches in general. The authors say the measures are not interchangeable, and the coach comparison rests on one coach of each type.",
  "paper": {
    "year": 2025,
    "citation": "Smith-Hale V, Mendoza R, Vargo C, Schoen M, Jimenez L, VanSumeren M, et al. Training Impulse and Session Ratings of Perceived Exertion as Perceived by Athletes and Observed by Coaches During Preseason Football Camp. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2025.",
    "doi": "10.1519/jsc.0000000000005169",
    "abstract": "Compared heart-rate training impulse with session RPE load from athletes, a football coach and a strength and conditioning coach during the first six practices of preseason camp in collegiate American football players, and examined first-year versus returning athletes and heart-rate recovery measures.",
    "tldr": "In one Division II football team's first six camp practices, athlete and coach ratings of session load tracked heart-rate load only moderately. Use ratings alongside heart-rate data, not as a substitute for it.",
    "methods": "Prospective study during the first six official practices of preseason camp; 29 athletes enrolled and 5 were excluded for missing 2 or more practices. Athletes wore chest-strap heart-rate monitors to calculate TRIMP and rated each session on the CR10 session RPE scale; the football and strength and conditioning coaches rated each athlete. Heart rate variability and resting heart rate were measured before practice. Pearson correlations and Mann-Whitney U tests were used.",
    "findings": "Across 139 observations, session loads correlated significantly with Edwards TRIMP: athletes r = 0.62, football coach r = 0.68 and strength and conditioning coach r = 0.49. Correlations were stronger in first-year athletes (0.68, 0.79, 0.64) than returning athletes (0.60, 0.70, 0.40). First-year athletes had a higher heart-rate load than returning athletes (median 780 vs 697), lower HRV and higher resting heart rate, but their own ratings did not differ (median 780 vs 735); the strength coach rated first-year athletes higher and the football coach rated them lower than returning players. HRV was inversely related to load (r = -0.29 for Edwards TRIMP) and resting heart rate positively related (r = 0.22), both small.",
    "limitations": "Small, unbalanced sample of 24 athletes and 2 coaches from one team over six practices, with maximal heart rate estimated for most athletes. The strength coach correlation is 0.49 in the abstract and results but 0.41 in the Discussion, and the Discussion's R2 of 0.17 matches 0.41, not 0.49. Figure 2 reports N = 129 observations versus 139 in the text, the Figure 3 caption reverses the group sizes, and Table 1 gives a combined body fat (29.96%) higher than both group means (30.82% and 25.6%), which is not possible. Results tables and text values were used here.",
    "practicalImplications": "Ratings and heart-rate load agree only moderately, so session RPE from athletes or coaches should not be treated as interchangeable with heart-rate monitoring. The authors suggest both kinds of measure add unique information and that feedback on heart rate may help coaches and athletes align their ratings, which this study did not test.",
    "athleteDev": "During preseason camp, athlete and football coach ratings tracked heart-rate load with low-to-moderate agreement. The single strength and conditioning coach, who had under one year with the program, agreed least, so the authors suggest strength staff need better information on cumulative field-practice load; this cannot be generalized beyond these two coaches.",
    "rtp": "The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It examined collegiate athletes in preseason practice and did not study injured or returning athletes or return-to-play decisions."
  },
  "verification": {
    "status": "CORRECTED",
    "changes": [
      "paper.limitations: added the R2 check showing the Discussion value fits r = 0.41, not 0.49 ('S&C (R2 = 0.17 ...)'; 'the SCC (r = 0.41)')",
      "paper.limitations: added the Figure 2 observation count conflict ('all observations (N = 129)' vs 'accumulated 139 total observations')",
      "paper.limitations: added impossible Table 1 combined body fat ('30.82 ... 25.6 ... 29.96')",
      "paper.findings: added subgroup correlations, first-year HRV/RHR differences and opposite coach rating differences ('SCC observed first-year athletes to have a greater TL'; 'FBC observed first-year athletes to have a lower TL')",
      "screeningLimitations/synthesisCaution/athleteDev: added that each coach type is n = 1 ('1 FBC (>10 years' experience...) and 1 SCC (<1-year experience...)')",
      "paper.methods: added enrollment and exclusion (29 enrolled, 5 excluded)"
    ],
    "residualConcerns": "Several internal numerical conflicts (SCC r 0.49 vs 0.41, N 139 vs 129, swapped Figure 3 group sizes, Table 1 body fat). Edwards TRIMP and athlete-rated load share the same first-year median (780), which may be a reporting error. Athlete sex is not stated explicitly, so no sex tag was added.",
    "spotCheckPriority": "high"
  }
}

{
  "id": "Q67",
  "sourceFile": "Velocity-based resistance training - Impact of velocity loss in the set on neuromuscular performance and hormonal response.pdf",
  "decision": "INCLUDE",
  "exclusionReason": "",
  "degradedReason": "",
  "doiMissing": false,
  "identityCheck": "PDF title 'Velocity-based resistance training: Impact of velocity loss in the set on neuromuscular performance and hormonal response' (Rodriguez-Rosell et al., Appl Physiol Nutr Metab accepted manuscript) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
  "confidence": "high",
  "studyDesign": "Randomized Controlled Trial",
  "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
  "domains": ["Training & Performance"],
  "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching"],
  "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
  "populations": ["Adult / Recreational"],
  "evidenceSummary": "Randomized two-group study of 25 young healthy men (10% velocity loss per set, n = 12; 30% velocity loss, n = 13) who trained twice weekly for 8 weeks with velocity-based full-squat sets at 70-85% 1RM. Both groups improved strength and the fatigue test similarly; the 10% group had larger percentage gains in countermovement jump and was the only group to improve 10 m and 20 m sprint time, despite about half the repetitions. The only significant time-by-group interactions were for sprint times; strength, jump, EMG and hormone changes did not differ significantly between groups.",
  "screeningLimitations": "Small sample of physically active sport science students with 1-3 years of resistance training, not athletes, with two training arms and no untrained control. Only the full squat was trained and tested, the 1RM was estimated from bar velocity, and most hormone and EMG changes were not significant. The dose-response curves combine four group means from this and an earlier study by the same group.",
  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the 10% velocity-loss result as proof that low-fatigue sets are superior for athletes in general. This was an 8-week study in active students; strength and jump differences between groups were not significant, and only sprint time differed by group.",
  "paper": {
    "year": 2020,
    "citation": "Rodríguez-Rosell D, Yáñez-García JM, Mora-Custodio R, Pareja-Blanco F, Ravelo-García AG, Ribas-Serna J, et al. Velocity-based resistance training: Impact of velocity loss in the set on neuromuscular performance and hormonal response. Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism. 2020.",
    "doi": "10.1139/apnm-2019-0829",
    "abstract": "Compared 10% and 30% velocity loss per set in an 8-week full-squat velocity-based program in 25 young men, measuring strength, jump, sprint, fatigue, knee extensor EMG, resting hormones and troponin T.",
    "tldr": "In physically active men, sets stopped at 10% velocity loss produced strength and jump gains similar to sets at 30%, with under half the repetitions. Only the 10% group improved sprint times, and troponin T rose in both groups, more in the 30% group.",
    "methods": "Randomized two-group, 8-week study. Participants were matched on estimated 1RM and randomly assigned. Both groups trained the full squat at 70-85% 1RM, three sets per session, twice weekly, with each set ended at 10% velocity loss or at a loss that progressed from 20% to 30% (average 29.4%). Pre and post tests included a 20 m sprint, countermovement jump, a progressive loading test with estimated 1RM, a fatigue test, knee extensor EMG and resting blood hormones.",
    "findings": "Compliance was 100%. Both groups improved estimated 1RM (VL10% +17.9%, VL30% +14.9%) and fatigue-test repetitions (+74.8% and +73.2%). Countermovement jump rose 9.2% in the 10% group and 5.4% in the 30% group, with a small, non-significant between-group effect (0.23). Sprint times for 10 m and 20 m improved only in the 10% group (-1.6% and -1.5%), with a significant time-by-group interaction. EMG changes were not significant in either group. Troponin T rose 59.9% (10%) and 128.4% (30%), significant within both groups; no other resting hormone changed significantly.",
    "limitations": "1RM was estimated from bar velocity rather than measured, and there was no untrained control group. The abstract says only the 10% group showed EMG increments, but the Results report no significant EMG change in either group. The Results state troponin T changes were significantly greater in the 30% group, yet also state there was no significant time-by-group interaction for any biochemical marker. The 10% group repetition total is given as 109.6 plus or minus 2.0 in the Results and plus or minus 12.0 in the Discussion. The PDF is an accepted manuscript with only a 2020 download stamp and no volume, issue or pages.",
    "practicalImplications": "Stopping sets at a set velocity loss is a practical way to control fatigue in a 70-85% 1RM squat program. Sets ended at 10% loss gave strength and fatigue-test gains similar to 30% loss with fewer repetitions and better sprint changes, so lower velocity-loss limits may suit programs that prioritize sprint and jump performance. This needs confirmation in trained athletes and with multi-exercise programs.",
    "athleteDev": "In this sample of active men, a 10% velocity-loss set (about 2 to 3 repetitions in practice) gave strength and fatigue-test gains similar to a 30% set, with only the 10% group improving sprint time, using about half the repetitions. Coaches could use velocity loss as a set-ending rule, but the study was short, used non-athletes, and did not measure sport performance.",
    "rtp": "The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested injury-free men in a laboratory training block and included no injured or rehabilitating participants."
  },
  "verification": {
    "status": "CORRECTED",
    "changes": [
      "paper.limitations: added the troponin T conflict ('changes in TnT protein were significantly greater in VL30% than in VL10%' vs 'There was no significant time x group interaction for any hormonal or biochemical marker')",
      "paper.tldr: 'only the 30% group showed a larger rise in troponin T' -> troponin T rose in both groups, more in the 30% group (Table 3: 59.9% ** and 128.4% ***)",
      "evidenceSummary/synthesisCaution: stated that sprint time was the only significant group interaction ('significant time x group interaction (p<0.05) for T10 and T20, whereas no significant ... for any strength variable or CMJ')",
      "paper.methods: added that the 30% group progressed from 20% to 30% loss ('the VL followed a progression from 20% to 30%, the average VL ... being 29.4 ± 1.3%')",
      "paper.athleteDev: repetitions per set 'about 2 to 4' -> about 2 to 3 as performed (Table 1 overall 2.3 ± 0.2; the authors' text says 2-4)",
      "screeningLimitations: added prior training experience and the pooled four-point dose-response curves ('results of both the present study and those obtained by Pareja-Blanco et al. (2017c) were used')"
    ],
    "residualConcerns": "Troponin T is reported in ng/mL with resting values of 3.4 to 7.9 ng/mL, which would be far above clinical cardiac thresholds; the unit is probably misprinted, and the authors interpret it as muscle damage although the cited source concerns cardiac biomarkers. Staff should not read this as cardiac injury from squat training. Accepted manuscript; final version may differ.",
    "spotCheckPriority": "high"
  }
}

  "sourceFile": "Vitamin C supplementation and athletic performance - A review.pdf",
  "decision": "INCLUDE",
  "exclusionReason": "",
  "degradedReason": "",
  "doiMissing": false,
  "identityCheck": "PDF title 'Vitamin C Supplementation and Athletic Performance: A Review' (Rogers, Lawlor and Moeller, Current Sports Medicine Reports) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
  "confidence": "high",
  "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
  "primaryDomain": "Nutrition & Hydration",
  "domains": ["Nutrition & Hydration", "Training & Performance", "Recovery & Readiness"],
  "audiences": ["Nutrition", "Performance", "Coaching"],
  "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
  "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
  "evidenceSummary": "Review of 14 double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trials of supraphysiologic vitamin C in athletes and active adults, identified by a PubMed search of 2012 to 2022 (97 articles screened). Only two trials used vitamin C alone; the rest combined it with vitamin E, quercetin or alpha-lipoic acid. The authors report that three trials found lower muscle damage markers with vitamin C-containing supplements, while the other 11 found neutral or negative effects on muscle damage, performance, soreness or training adaptation.",
  "screeningLimitations": "The review is a single PubMed search with a narrow keyword set, no meta-analysis and no formal quality grading. Most trials were small and combined vitamin C with other antioxidants, so vitamin C effects cannot be separated. The summary table and text disagree on several trial details.",
  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this as showing that vitamin C itself blunts training adaptation, when the adaptation findings come from vitamin C plus vitamin E trials, mostly small, and in one case rest on within-group rather than between-group results.",
  "paper": {
    "year": 2023,
    "citation": "Rogers DR, Lawlor DJ, Moeller JL. Vitamin C Supplementation and Athletic Performance: A Review. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2023;22(7):255-259.",
    "doi": "10.1249/jsr.0000000000001083",
    "abstract": "Reviews 14 randomized placebo-controlled trials of high-dose vitamin C in athletes and active people, most combined with other antioxidants, on muscle damage, performance and training adaptation.",
    "tldr": "Across 14 placebo-controlled trials, high-dose vitamin C showed no consistent benefit for performance or soreness, and some trials reported blunted training adaptations when taken with vitamin E. The authors advise against long-term high-dose vitamin C and recommend antioxidants from a nutrient-rich diet.",
    "methods": "PubMed search for 2012 to 2022 using the terms vitamin C, ascorbic acid, athlete and performance, yielding 97 articles. Inclusion required a double-blind placebo-controlled randomized trial of supraphysiologic vitamin C (alone or mixed) and an exercise performance or muscle damage outcome. Fourteen trials were included and summarized narratively with no pooled analysis.",
    "findings": "Three trials reported lower muscle damage markers: vitamin C plus quercetin (Askari), short-term vitamin C plus vitamin E around taekwondo competition (Chou), and vitamin C plus vitamin E in elite endurance athletes (Gillam), although in Gillam the lower creatine kinase tracked vitamin E levels, not vitamin C. Other trials found no benefit for performance, soreness or perceived exertion, and a pre-exercise combined antioxidant reduced cycling power in hyperoxia. With long-term vitamin C plus vitamin E, placebo groups gained more lean mass and muscle thickness than supplemented groups in older men (between-group), and showed greater mitochondrial biogenesis markers in two endurance studies; in recreational weightlifters only the placebo group improved strength and hypertrophy from baseline, with no reported between-group difference.",
    "limitations": "Single search and no formal quality appraisal. Most trials co-supplemented vitamin C with other antioxidants, so vitamin C effects cannot be isolated, and samples are small. The table and text disagree on the 10-week Martinez-Ferran sample (32 vs 12), vitamin E dose in Paulsen (235 vs 325 mg) and de Oliveira (235 mg vs 400 IU), Morrison duration (8 vs 4 weeks), Askari population (students vs athletes) and Chou myoglobin p-value (0.021 vs 0.016); the text also says ten trials used vitamin E while the table lists eleven.",
    "practicalImplications": "Athletes asking about high-dose vitamin C for performance or recovery should be told the trial evidence is inconsistent, and that the authors advise against long-term high-dose supplementation because combined vitamin C and E may blunt training adaptations. Diet is the recommended source of antioxidants. Short-term use around competition is listed by the authors as a research gap.",
    "athleteDev": "The review supports the authors' advice against long-term high-dose vitamin C during training blocks, but the blunting evidence comes from vitamin C plus vitamin E trials. Acute high-dose use has not shown a consistent performance benefit.",
    "rtp": "The review contains no return-to-sport or injury-recovery trials. Three small trials reported lower muscle damage markers after exercise, but they were not injury studies, and the authors do not recommend long-term high-dose use. These findings cannot support rehabilitation or return-to-sport use."
  },
  "verification": {
    "status": "CORRECTED",
    "changes": [
      "paper.findings: 'placebo groups had larger gains ... in strength and hypertrophy in recreational weightlifters' -> within-group gains in placebo only, no between-group difference reported ('found no significant difference in muscle strength or hypertrophy, whereas the placebo group showed statistically significant gains ... compared with baseline values')",
      "paper.findings: Gillam benefit attributed to vitamin E, not vitamin C ('No change in serum ascorbate or effect of vitamin C on post-run CK was noted (P > 0.1)')",
      "paper.limitations: added table-text conflicts for de Oliveira vitamin E dose (table 235 mg, text 400 IU), Morrison duration (table 8 wk, text 4 wk), Askari population (table 'male students', text 'male athletes'), Chou myoglobin p (0.021 vs 0.016) and the vitamin E trial count (text ten, table eleven)",
      "synthesisCaution/athleteDev: reframed so the blunting claim is tied to vitamin C plus vitamin E trials",
      "evidenceSummary: specified that only two trials used vitamin C alone ('only two of the studies supplemented with vitamin C alone')"
    ],
    "residualConcerns": "Many internal table-text discrepancies suggest transcription errors in the source review; trial-level details should be checked against the primary trials before citing them. Coded as Systematic Review per library precedent (described search and inclusion criteria), though the authors title it a review and do no appraisal.",
    "spotCheckPriority": "high"
  }
}

{
  "id": "Q70",
  "sourceFile": "Vitamin D for improved bone health and prevention of stress fractures - A review of the literature.pdf",
  "decision": "INCLUDE",
  "exclusionReason": "",
  "degradedReason": "",
  "doiMissing": false,
  "identityCheck": "PDF title 'Vitamin D for Improved Bone Health and Prevention of Stress Fractures: A Review of the Literature' (Lawley, Syrop and Fredericson, Current Sports Medicine Reports) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
  "confidence": "high",
  "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
  "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
  "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Nutrition & Hydration"],
  "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Nutrition"],
  "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
  "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
  "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of vitamin D status, bone health and stress fractures, drawing on trials, cohort and case-control studies in children, adults, military recruits and some athletes. The authors report a consistent but heterogeneous association between vitamin D status and stress fracture, with a meta-analysis of eight military studies finding lower 25(OH)D in stress fracture cases (mean difference -2.44 ng/mL, 95% CI -4.05 to -0.84). They recommend vitamin D3 to maintain status in athletes at high stress-fracture risk, but say the data do not support a specific dose or target level for athletes.",
  "screeningLimitations": "No search method is described, so the selection of studies cannot be checked. The authors note that placebo-controlled RCTs in athletes are scarce, and most athlete evidence is observational. Many bone-outcome trials were in children, postmenopausal women or older adults, and the stress-fracture meta-analysis used military personnel rather than sport athletes. Vitamin D thresholds differ across organizations and no validated assay is available.",
  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this as proof that vitamin D supplementation prevents stress fractures in athletes. The athlete evidence is mainly observational, the only prevention trial cited combined calcium and vitamin D in Navy recruits, the female-athlete hazard ratio the authors call protective has a confidence interval crossing 1, and a large meta-analysis found no fracture prevention in older adults.",
  "paper": {
    "year": 2020,
    "citation": "Lawley R, Syrop IP, Fredericson M. Vitamin D for Improved Bone Health and Prevention of Stress Fractures: A Review of the Literature. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2020;19(6):202-208.",
    "doi": "10.1249/jsr.0000000000000718",
    "abstract": "Reviews vitamin D physiology, status measurement and bone health, then the evidence linking vitamin D status and supplementation with stress fractures in adolescents, military recruits and athletes.",
    "tldr": "Vitamin D status and stress fracture risk appear linked in athletes and recruits, but the studies are heterogeneous and mostly observational. The authors recommend vitamin D3 to maintain status in high-risk athletes, but the review does not set a dose or target level for them.",
    "methods": "Narrative literature review. The article does not describe a search strategy, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal.",
    "findings": "Indoor athletes are at greater risk of low 25(OH)D, though insufficiency is also reported in outdoor athletes and one study of female distance runners found mostly adequate status. A meta-analysis of eight military studies (2,634 personnel) found lower 25(OH)D in stress fracture cases, and cohorts of Finnish and Royal Marine recruits linked lower baseline 25(OH)D to stress fracture. In 37 British Army recruits, recovery from lower-limb stress fracture took about 10 weeks with sufficient 25(OH)D, 12 with insufficient and 13 with deficient levels. In female Navy recruits, 2000 mg calcium plus 800 IU vitamin D for 8 weeks gave a 20% lower stress fracture incidence, and in young female runners vitamin D intake gave an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.67 (0.34 to 1.31).",
    "limitations": "No search method or quality appraisal is described. Athlete evidence is mostly observational and small, and the authors describe a non-significant hazard ratio (CI 0.34 to 1.31) as protective. Bone density trials in children and older adults are mixed, and a meta-analysis of 81 RCTs found no fracture or meaningful BMD benefit in older adults. Vitamin D thresholds differ by organization, and the authors note that 25(OH)D may not be the best marker.",
    "practicalImplications": "The authors recommend vitamin D3 to maintain 25(OH)D status in athletes at high stress-fracture risk and cite thresholds of supplementing below 30 ng/mL (Shuler) or keeping 32 to 50 ng/mL (Female Athlete Triad Coalition), with 800 to 2000 IU daily suggested for high-risk individuals in a cited concept review. They state the athlete data are not strong enough to support a specific dose or target. Vitamin D is described as safe above usual intakes, though one trial reported more kidney stones in women.",
    "athleteDev": "The review does not support a dose or target serum level for athletic performance. It cites Cannell's suggestion that 50 ng/mL may be ideal for performance, but the authors say the athlete data are not strong enough to set a dose or target for bone health.",
    "rtp": "The only recovery data are military: 37 recruits with sufficient 25(OH)D recovered from lower-limb stress fractures faster than those insufficient or deficient. This does not give a return-to-sport protocol, and the review cannot set return-to-play criteria or a dosing plan for an injured athlete."
  },
  "verification": {
    "status": "CORRECTED",
    "changes": [
      "paper.findings: 'Athletes, especially indoor and endurance athletes, often have low 25(OH)D' -> indoor athletes at greater risk; the cited female distance runner study found adequate status ('59 female distance runners ... observed adequate vitamin D status with only 18.6% insufficient or deficient')",
      "paper.practicalImplications: removed unsupported advice to screen athletes including 'those with prior fracture' and 'military-type trainees'; replaced with the authors' actual recommendation and cited thresholds ('we recommend vitamin D3 supplementation to maintain 25(OH)D status, especially in athletes at high risk of stress fracture')",
      "paper.findings/limitations/synthesisCaution: added the Nieves hazard ratio whose CI crosses 1 although called protective ('adjusted hazard ratio of 0.67 (0.34 to 1.31)')",
      "paper.findings: Navy trial specified as female recruits, calcium 2000 mg plus 800 IU vitamin D for 8 wk, combined intervention ('2000 mg calcium and 800 international units of vitamin D versus placebo for 8 wk')",
      "paper.practicalImplications: added safety note on kidney stones ('one reported an absolute increase in kidney stones in women')"
    ],
    "residualConcerns": "The text cites the Dao military meta-analysis as reference 48 (Miller) in places, a citation-number error in the source. Bone stress injury in athletes is clinically relevant; dosing statements come from cited reviews, not trials in athletes.",
    "spotCheckPriority": "high"
  }
}

  "domains": ["Recovery & Readiness", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],

  "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of whole-body cryotherapy (WBC) in sports medicine, covering inflammation, muscle damage, bone, blood, hormone and lipid markers, functional recovery, clinical use in arthritis and adhesive capsulitis, and safety. The authors report anti-inflammatory and lipid changes, mixed creatine kinase and blood findings, and limited, mixed results for functional recovery and performance, which they summarize as relatively weak but supportive evidence for recovery.",
  "screeningLimitations": "No search method or quality appraisal is described, so the selection of studies cannot be checked. content.text:
I've written all eight records to `verified/Q65.json` through `verified/Q72.json`. All eight are marked CORRECTED and none of the decisions changed. Identity, the external DOI and the year match Crossref for every paper. My working text copies are in `helpers/v09/`.

- **Q65**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. Fixed how the anxiety and osteoarthritis evidence was described, and replaced the dosing advice with what the authors actually say ("600 mg of CBD is not a good choice"). Flagged high because it covers concussion and cannabinoids.
- **Q66**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. Checked the number conflicts against the tables and recorded them all:
  - The strength coach correlation is r = 0.49 in the results but 0.41 in the Discussion, and the Discussion's R² of 0.17 fits 0.41.
  - Figure 2 says N = 129 observations; the text says 139.
  - The Figure 3 caption swaps the group sizes.
  - Table 1's combined body fat (29.96%) is higher than both group means, which can't be right.

  I also noted that each coach type is a single person.
- **Q67**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. The paper says troponin T rose more in the 30% group, but also says no biochemical marker had a significant group difference. Sprint time is the only real between-group effect. The troponin unit (ng/mL) looks misprinted, so it should not be read as cardiac injury.
- **Q68**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, normal. Fixed overstated claims about velocity below 1.0 m/s and about reliability: only one CV was over 10%, and ICCs range from 0.77 to 0.99. Each load had three single repetitions. The authors' peak-velocity advice is now labelled as their interpretation, not a tested result.
- **Q69**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. The draft said placebo groups gained more strength and muscle size in the weightlifter trial; that was a within-group change only. In the Gillam trial the lower creatine kinase tracked vitamin E, not vitamin C. The draft listed two table–text conflicts and I found six more, including vitamin E doses, Morrison's duration (8 vs 4 weeks) and two p-values.
- **Q70**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. The draft said endurance athletes are often low in vitamin D, which the text contradicts. I removed screening advice the authors don't give. I also flagged that the hazard ratio the authors call protective (0.67, 95% CI 0.34 to 1.31) is not significant, and that the Navy trial combined calcium with vitamin D.
- **Q71**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. The draft said "most controlled trials found no benefit." The text actually reports mixed results, with four positive and three negative sources, and the authors call the evidence "relatively weak, but supportive." I also added the two reported complications.
- **Q72**: EXCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. The commentary call stands: it is a section-by-section critique of the single 2016 Berlin concussion consensus statement, plus the authors' own opinions. It is borderline, though, because its abstract says "We review." I added the year, citation and DOI, which the batch rule requires whenever identity matches.
